routes.label: Group by the first return to ground
Recur on hop count and height

question:
Buzz Bunny is hopping up and down a set of stairs, one step at a time. In how many ways can Buzz start on the ground, make a sequence of \(6\) hops, and end up back on the ground? (For example, one sequence of hops is up-up-down-down-up-down.)

[Figure 1](figures/2024_AMC_8_Q13_fig1.png)
solution:
To return to ground, Buzz needs equally many up-hops and down-hops, so he must make three of each. Write \(U\) for an up-hop and \(D\) for a down-hop. He cannot go below ground, so his first hop must be \(U\), and his final hop must be \(D\).

Group the sequences by the second hop.

If the second hop is \(D\), Buzz begins with \(UD\) and is back on the ground. The remaining four hops must start with \(U\) and end with \(D\). The two middle hops must be one \(U\) and one \(D\), in either order. Both orders are allowed, giving
\[
\mathrm{UDUUDD},\qquad \mathrm{UDUDUD}.
\]

If the second hop is \(U\), Buzz begins with \(UU\). If his third hop is also \(U\), all three remaining hops must be \(D\). If his third hop is \(D\), he is on the first stair with one up-hop and two down-hops left. Their possible orders are \(UDD\), \(DUD\), and \(DDU\), but \(DDU\) would take him below ground. This gives
\[
\mathrm{UUUDDD},\qquad \mathrm{UUDUDD},\qquad \mathrm{UUDDUD}.
\]

The two cases cover every possible second hop and cannot overlap. The five listed sequences are distinct and all stay at or above ground. Thus there are \(2+3=\boxed{5}\) ways, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
